L20: # Replayable Authority Histories for Auditing Automated Agents
L21: ## 【0†Abstract】
L22: Software agents act on authority that changes while they run: permissions are granted and revoked, running instances are replaced, and some requests are refused. Activity logs record what a system reports it did, but they do not by themselves show what an agent was allowed to do when it acted, and the operator can edit them.
L23: This document specifies a model for an authority history: an append-only, signed record of who granted what to whom, which actions were admitted, which requests were refused, and which unfinished duties survive when one agent replaces another. Given independently authenticated owner keys and history identity, a verifier can replay the history and recompute its recorded authorization decisions while trusting neither the agent nor the operator.
L24: The document states what such a verifier can and cannot establish. Optional profiles cover external anchoring, federated operation, human-attested keys and zero-knowledge disclosure. An informative appendix describes one encoding.【1†¶】

L12: # About the security of the 1Password Account Trust Log
L13: 
L14: About the security of the 1Password Account Trust Log Learn how the Account Trust Log protects your secrets from everyone, including 1Password.Security and privacy 1Password features
L15: The Account Trust Log is a cryptographic record of trust in a 1Password account that allows services like 【1†Automated Provisioning】 to verify the authenticity of public keys used to share sensitive data, without needing to trust 1Password’s servers. The log allows clients to verify a public key before carrying out operations with that key. Even if 1Password’s infrastructure were compromised or behaving maliciously, attackers couldn’t insert themselves into a key exchange without your knowledge.
L16: After the Trust Log is turned on, it runs in the background. Unless malicious activity is detected, no user action is required to stay protected.
L17: ## Design principles
L18: 
L19: The Account Trust Log system is designed around these core principles:
L20:   * Zero server trust: Once configured, clients no longer need to rely on the server for genuine public keys.
L21:   * Immutable: Data written to the Trust Log can’t be removed or modified by anyone, including 1Password.
L22:   * Transparent and auditable: The log is verifiable from the beginning and provides a permanent audit trail of account activity.
L23:   * Privacy-preserving: No private data is stored in the Trust Log.
L24:   * Foundational: You can rely on the Trust Log for the newest 1Password features. The Trust Log cannot be turned off once it’s enabled, so it acts as a permanent security upgrade to an account.
L25: ## Trust principles
L26: 
L27: The Trust Log is a cryptographically linked series of entries which form a tamper-evident chain describing which keys are trusted in an account over its lifetime. Events that add a trusted public key, such as adding a user or group, are recorded as entries. Verification is distributed across 1Password clients and coordinated by 1Password’s servers, so there’s no single arbiter of truth that could be compromised alone.
L28: Every entry is signed by a trusted key in the log’s context, so only authorized actors can change account state. When an admin confirms a new user, they sign an entry with a signing key they own. That entry is trusted only if the admin was added to the log earlier and not later removed. Changes to the Trust Log therefore come from within the account, with trust rooted in the first owner who created the account.
L29: The Trust Log provides cryptographic attribution for sensitive security events. Unlike standard audit logs, every Trust Log entry is signed with the user’s private key, which is encrypted and protected by their 【2†Account Unlock Key.†agilebits.github.io】 This makes sure that actions are permanently and verifiably linked to the specific individual, because only they can access the private key required to sign an entry.
L30: ### Trust on first use
L31: 
L32: The Trust Log follows a “Trust on first use” model. When the Trust Log is enabled, you initially trust that existing account data is correct. After that, you no longer need to trust the server for key authenticity. Clients keep some local state about the Trust Log so they can detect if the server suddenly pretends the Trust Log isn’t turned on, attempts to alter an entry that’s already been validated, or provides data not signed by another admin in the account.
L33: ### World State
L34: 
L35: Alongside the Trust Log, the system defines a World State. This is another tamper-evident structure that clients use to look up trusted data for sensitive operations (for example, encrypting a shared secret). The World State is derived from Trust Log history up to a point in time, so there’s one World State per trust log entry.
L36: The Trust Log records how the account changes over time, while the World State is a snapshot of all trusted data at a moment in time. Each entry stores its World State’s integrity value, so the two structures stay tightly coupled.
L37: 
L38: The following are some important properties of the World State:
L39: 
L40:   * A complete Trust Log can always be replayed, entry by entry, to reconstruct a World State.
L41:   * The World State has a canonical form: Each Trust Log entry corresponds to exactly one World State.
L42: The World State is implemented as a 【3†Modified Patricia-Merkle Trie (MPT)†ethereum.org】, which is a type of 【4†radix trie.†en.wikipedia.org】 MPTs fit this use case because they’re efficient to store and query, while also being deterministic, verifiable, and flexible in what they store.
L43: ## Appending to the Trust Log
L44: 
L45: An easy way to understand the Trust Log as a verifiable chain is to see how a new entry is built and appended.
L46: ### Entry structure
L47: 
L48: Each Trust Log entry includes the following:
L49: 
L50:   * Operation: The change the entry makes to the World State.
L51:   * Entry integrity: A hash of the previous entry in the chain.
L52:   * Signature: Authentication of who created the entry.
L53:   * Metadata: Extra context about the entry.
L54: 
L55: Because each new entry includes the previous entry’s hash, clients can verify the full history. Changing any entry invalidates the integrity of every later entry, so tampering is detectable.
L56: ### Appending a new entry
L57: 
L58: Appending starts from the latest Trust Log entry (HEAD) and its World State:
L59: 
L60: 【5†Image: A diagram showing the latest entry in the Trust Log and its World State.】
L61: 
L62: A new Operation is built from the action being performed. The rules for how an Operation updates the World State are precise and shared by all clients. Applying the Operation to the current World State yields the new World State and its integrity value:
L63: 【6†Image: A diagram showing the path from the action in the Trust Log to the current World State and the new World State based on the operation.】
L64: Using the new World State integrity, the HEAD’s integrity, and other metadata, the new entry is assembled. The inclusion of the HEAD entry’s integrity makes sure that the new entry forms a new link in the chain of the Trust Log. The contents of the new entry will be used by clients to make sure the entry was a valid operation at the time it was created and hasn’t been tampered with since.
L65: The new entry is serialized, signed, and sent to the server to append to the account’s Trust Log and distribute to everyone on the account:
L66: 
L67: 【7†Image: A diagram showing the path from the new entry to the latest entry, then the World State.】

L69: 
L70: As the Trust Log grows, each client must track the account’s current trusted state. Updating local state to match the latest shared log is called fast-forwarding.

L39: # Bitcoin-Anchored Temporal Proof for Transparency Services
L40: ## 【19†Abstract】
L41: 
L42: This document defines a mechanism for temporal anchoring of digital artifacts by committing cryptographic hashes to the Bitcoin blockchain via the OpenTimestamps protocol. The resulting proof is independently verifiable by any party with access to independently validated Bitcoin chain data, without contacting the anchoring service. The SCITT Architecture is used as the primary integration example. No changes to the SCITT architecture are required.【20†¶】
